name: Dirichlet Process
analogy: Think of it as a restaurant with unlimited tables. Each new diner joins a table with probability in proportion to how many are already seated there, or occasionally opens a new table. Popular tables grow, rare ones stay small, and the number of tables is decided by the data instead of being fixed in advance.

steps.title: Describe each bar by a few numbers
steps.description: Turn each bar into a short row of features that say what kind of market it is in, such as return, range and volume. These rows are what get grouped into regimes.
steps.inExample: Each of the last 500 MNQ 5-minute bars is described by its return, its range in points against the average true range, and its volume against the 20-bar average.

steps.title: Set how eager the process is to create new groups
steps.description: A single setting, the concentration, controls how readily a new group is started. A small value gives few groups; a larger value allows more.
steps.inExample: The concentration is 1, which for 500 bars favours a handful of regimes.

steps.title: Assign each bar to a group or a new one
steps.description: For each bar, the chance of joining an existing group grows with the size of the group and with how well the bar fits its typical values. There is also a chance, set by the concentration, of starting a brand new group.
steps.inExample: Bar 312 has a range of 45 points and volume 110 percent above average. It is a good fit for the large-move group of 85 bars and a poor fit for the quiet group of 230 bars.

steps.title: Re-estimate what each group looks like
steps.description: After assignments change, each group's typical values and spread are recomputed from the bars now in it. A new group starts from a broad prior guess and is sharpened as bars join.
steps.inExample: The large-move group's average range rises slightly now that bar 312 has joined it.

steps.title: Sweep through all bars many times
steps.description: Steps three and four repeat over every bar, hundreds of times. Groups that lose their bars disappear, and groups that gain them settle. The process ends with a stable set of groups.
steps.inExample: After 300 sweeps the 500 bars are in four groups of 230, 155, 85 and 30 bars, which are 46, 31, 17 and 6 percent of the bars.

steps.title: Score a new bar against the groups
steps.description: A new bar gets a probability for each existing group, and a probability of belonging to a completely new one. A high chance of a new group flags an unusual bar.
steps.inExample: The latest bar gets 62 percent for the large-move group, 21 percent for the trending group, 9 percent for the small group, 4 percent for the quiet group and 4 percent for a new group.

useFor.task: Discovering how many regimes there are
useFor.example: Letting MNQ and ES bars sort themselves into quiet, trending and wild regimes without choosing the number of regimes beforehand.
Treating a bar with a high chance of starting its own group as a candidate anomaly, such as a news spike.
Using the spread of the current regime to size stops and targets, wider in a wild regime and tighter in a quiet one.

useFor.task: Providing a regime label to other models
useFor.example: Feeding the most likely regime as a categorical input to a gradient-boosted direction classifier.

avoidWhen: You already know there are exactly two or three regimes and want fast, simple fitting; a fixed-size mixture model or a hidden Markov model is cheaper and easier to explain.
Regime order and persistence matter, such as how long a regime tends to last; this model treats bars as unordered, so a hidden Markov model that models switching is the better fit.

example.scenario: A researcher groups the last 500 MNQ 5-minute bars into regimes without fixing how many, then scores the latest bar to see which regime it belongs to and whether it looks like something new.

input.summary: A window of bars described by three numbers each, the concentration setting and the latest bar's values.

fields.name: bars in the window
fields.meaning: The history the regimes are learned from.

fields.name: features per bar
fields.value: return, range in points, volume ratio
fields.meaning: The three numbers describing each bar.

fields.name: concentration
fields.meaning: How eagerly new groups are started.

fields.name: latest bar range
fields.meaning: About 80 percent above a typical average true range of 25 points.

fields.name: latest bar volume
fields.meaning: Trading was heavy in the latest bar.

fields.name: latest bar return
fields.value: down about a fifth of a percent
fields.meaning: Close versus open of the bar, roughly 35 points on a price near 19,500.

output.summary: The regimes found, their sizes, and the latest bar's regime probabilities.

fields.name: regimes found
fields.meaning: Quiet, trending, large-move and a small unusual group.

fields.name: regime sizes
fields.meaning: Which are 46, 31, 17 and 6 percent of the window.

fields.name: latest bar probability, large-move regime
fields.meaning: The most likely regime for the latest bar.

fields.name: latest bar probability, other regimes
fields.meaning: The rest of the probability across existing regimes.

fields.name: latest bar probability of a new regime
fields.meaning: A low value means the bar looks like something already seen.

example.reading: The large-move regime is the best guess at 62 percent, so widen stops and size down accordingly. A new-regime chance of 4 percent says the bar is ordinary for this window. The regimes are descriptive labels learned from past bars; check that they persist on later data before relying on them.
